newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no Hebron boost for Israel-Syria talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no Hebron boost for Israel-Syria talks.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Thursday it saw no sign so far that Wednesday's Hebron agreement between Israel and the Palestinians would help to revive stalled Israeli-Syrian peace talks.

"I think this negotiation stands on its own," department spokesman Nicholas Burns said of the Hebron deal, under which Israeli troops are to withdraw this month from most of Hebron, and from other West Bank areas by late next year.
"Obviously, the United States has had as a long-term goal the reinvigoration of the Syrian-Israeli peace negotiations. Do we think that those are imminent? No, we don't," Burns told a news briefing.
U.S.-brokered Israeli-Syrian negotiations, begun in 1991, have been frozen since early last year over the future of the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

Prospects for their resumption dipped further when right-wing Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu became Israeli Prime Minister last June. Likud policy guidelines say Israel must maintain sovereignty over the strategic Golan plateau.
The hard-won Hebron deal has led to some speculation that Netanyahu's apparent flexibility over the West Bank could be matched by similar concessions over the Golan.
But Burns said in response to a question: "I am purposely saying I can't draw you an intellectual link at this point. You have to see what happens here."

He said it was up to Israel and Syria "to make the fundamental decision of whether or not they want to engage in formal discussions or informal discussions. I don't believe that either government has made that decision right now."
Syria has so far not commented on the Hebron agreement, although Damascus-based Palestinian radical groups have attacked it and vowed to wreck it.
Meanwhile, President Bill Clinton on Thursday thanked Jordan's King Hussein and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak for their support for the Hebron accord.
National Security Adviser-designate Samuel Berger told network radio reporters that Clinton made morning phone calls to the two leaders thanking them for their roles.

Berger said the Hebron deal would not have been possible without the two Arab leaders. King Hussein kept talks between Israel and the Palestinians from collapsing last weekend with a compromise proposal.
Hussein, Mubarak, Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat are all expected to visit the White House separately in the coming months, but Berger said no summit was planned.
"This is not a big summit. This will be a series of meetings," he said.
